uncited: *   **Quantization Table:** A static array of 240 precomputed unit vectors.
These vectors correspond to the centers of gravity of the 240 triangles in the tessellated sphere.
*   **Index Mapping:** A lookup mechanism (e.g., a hash map or spatial partitioning) to map an input vector to one of the 240 indices.
**Generate Base Geometry:** Start with a regular dodecahedron inscribed in a unit sphere.
**Initial Tessellation:** Subdivide the dodecahedron into 60 triangles.
**Recursive Subdivision:** Subdivide each of the 60 triangles into four smaller triangles.
**Compute Centers:** Calculate the center of gravity (centroid) for each of the 240 triangles.
Determine which of the 240 triangles on the sphere the vector $\mathbf{g}$ falls into.
*   **Hardware Limits:** Standard hardware color maps often support 256 entries.
*   **Time Complexity:** Quantization is $O(N)$ where $N=240$ is the number of normals, or $O(1)$ if a spatial hash or lookup table is used to map vectors to indices.
*   **Memory Complexity:** The quantization table requires storage for 240 vectors.
If stored as 3 floats per vector, this is $240 \times 12 = 2880$ bytes.
If stored as indices into a 256-entry color map, it is negligible.
*   **When to use:** When a static, uniform normal quantization is sufficient and hardware supports 256-entry color maps.
*   **When not to use:** When data-dependent optimization is required for better visual quality (use Simulated Annealing variant) or when higher precision is needed.
